name: Ancient Egyptian religion
date_note: c.; last temple (Philae) closed c. 537 CE
making_significance: Egyptian religion drove the production of temples, divine statues, amulets, coffins and Books of the Dead by temple and funerary workshops.
materials_techniques: stone carving; faience; cartonnage; papyrus illustration; mummification
object_types: amulets; coffins; Books of the Dead; votive bronzes
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;record and writing
leaves_out: household and popular piety; Nubian forms of the same gods; human remains treated as objects
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Brooklyn Museum (CC BY where marked);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Human remains and funerary material hidden by default.

name: Mesopotamian religion
other_names: Sumerian, Akkadian, Babylonian and Assyrian religion
date_note: c.; temple cults to the Parthian period
making_significance: Mesopotamian temples commissioned cult statues, votive figures, foundation deposits and incantation bowls and ran large workshops.
materials_techniques: stone and copper-alloy votive figures; clay tablets; foundation pegs
object_types: votive statues; foundation pegs; incantation texts
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;record and writing
leaves_out: household cults; the temple-dependent labourers; neighbouring religions
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative;Wikimedia Commons

name: Greco-Roman religion
making_significance: Greek and Roman cults paid for temples, cult statues, votive offerings and sacrificial equipment, sustaining sculptors, bronze-casters and potters.
materials_techniques: marble and bronze sculpture; terracotta votives; temple building
leaves_out: mystery cults and local deities; enslaved temple workers; Christian destruction and reuse
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Getty Museum Open Content (public-domain images);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Norse religion
making_significance: Norse religion shaped picture stones, amulets such as Thor's hammers, ship burials and carved ornament.
materials_techniques: stone carving; silver casting; woodcarving
object_types: picture stones; hammer amulets; ship burials
defined_by: historians; Snorri Sturluson (13th c. Christian writer)
leaves_out: Sámi religion alongside; enslaved people in burials; modern nationalist misuse
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;SMK Denmark (public domain);Nationalmuseum Sweden (public domain)
notes: Watch for far-right appropriation of symbols.

name: Zoroastrianism
making_significance: Zoroastrian practice built fire temples and towers of silence and, among Parsis in India, patronised embroidered gara saris and silver ritual vessels.
materials_techniques: fire-temple building; silverwork; silk embroidery
object_types: fire altars; ritual vessels; gara saris
leaves_out: Irani Zoroastrians under persecution; converts' descendants; funerary practice
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;community-published site

name: Manichaeism
date_note: c.; Mani's preaching from 240; last traces in south China c. 16th c.
making_significance: Manichaeans used richly illuminated books and painting as teaching, including silk paintings from Turfan and south China.
materials_techniques: manuscript illumination; silk painting
leaves_out: a persecuted faith known mostly from its enemies' texts
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;International Dunhuang Programme (link out; check terms)

name: Judaism
making_significance: Jewish practice commissions Torah scrolls, ritual silver (Torah ornaments, Hanukkah lamps), synagogue buildings and illuminated Haggadot, often from Jewish and non-Jewish makers alike.
materials_techniques: scribal writing on parchment; silversmithing; embroidery; illumination
leaves_out: makers barred from guilds in many places; Beta Israel, Yemeni and other non-European traditions; objects looted 1933–45
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);British Library digitised collections (public-domain items);NYPL Digital Collections (public-domain items);Wikimedia Commons

name: Coptic Orthodox Christianity
making_significance: Coptic monasteries and churches commissioned icons, textiles, carved wood and manuscripts, including the well-known Coptic tapestry-woven tunic fragments.
materials_techniques: tapestry weaving in wool and linen; icon painting; woodcarving
functions: ritual and belief;clothing and adornment;record and writing
leaves_out: the dead whose burial textiles fill museums; Muslim makers of church fittings
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Brooklyn Museum (CC BY where marked);Wikimedia Commons

name: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Christianity
making_significance: The Ethiopian church sustains parchment manuscripts, painted icons and diptychs, processional crosses and rock-hewn churches.
materials_techniques: parchment making; tempera painting; metal casting; rock-cutting
functions: ritual and belief;record and writing;rule and display
leaves_out: Muslim and Beta Israel neighbours; tabots that must not be seen by laypeople
free_sources: Walters Art Museum (CC0);Met Open Access (CC0);British Library digitised collections (public-domain items);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Tabots are never displayed; some taken at Maqdala (1868) have been returned by churches (e.g. Edinburgh 2002); verify others.

name: Eastern Orthodox Christianity (Byzantine rite)
making_significance: Orthodox practice centres on icons, iconostases, mosaics, frescoes and embroidered liturgical textiles, and its Iconoclast controversy (726–843) fought over images.
materials_techniques: icon painting in tempera; mosaic; fresco; gold embroidery
leaves_out: Iconoclasts' losses; non-Orthodox subjects; icons taken as war booty
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Walters Art Museum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Latin (Roman) Catholic Christianity
making_significance: Catholic patronage commissioned cathedrals, altarpieces, reliquaries, vestments and devotional prints and, through missions, colonial church art worldwide.
materials_techniques: stained glass; panel painting; goldsmithing; embroidery; printing
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;record and writing
leaves_out: Indigenous and African makers of mission art; Reformation destruction; objects taken from colonised peoples by missionaries
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Rijksmuseum (CC0);National Gallery of Art Washington (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Protestant Christianities
making_significance: Protestant reform destroyed many images (iconoclasm) while promoting printed Bibles, hymnals and plain meeting houses, and missions spread print and dress codes.
materials_techniques: printing; engraving; plain carpentry
leaves_out: Catholic makers whose work was destroyed; missionised peoples told to abandon their images
free_sources: Rijksmuseum (CC0);Library of Congress (public-domain items);Wikimedia Commons

name: Shakers
other_names: United Society of Believers in Christ's Second Appearing
making_significance: The Shakers made plain furniture, oval boxes and tools whose simplicity later influenced modern designers.
materials_techniques: joinery; bentwood boxes; broom making
leaves_out: the women who led the society; its celibate community's survival
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items);Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: Armenian Apostolic Christianity
making_significance: The Armenian church produced carved khachkar cross-stones, stone churches and illuminated gospels, many destroyed in and after 1915.
materials_techniques: stone carving; manuscript illumination
leaves_out: makers killed or displaced in the genocide; khachkars destroyed at Julfa (1998–2006)
free_sources: Walters Art Museum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: West Syriac Christianity
making_significance: Syriac-speaking churches produced illuminated gospels such as the Rabbula Gospels (586) and monasteries such as Deir al-Za'faran.
materials_techniques: manuscript illumination; stone building
leaves_out: Syriac Christians displaced in 1915 (Sayfo) and since 2003
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;British Library digitised collections (public-domain items)

name: Church of the East
date_note: c.; continues as Assyrian Church of the East
making_significance: The Church of the East spread from Mesopotamia to China, leaving the Xi'an stele (781), Turfan paintings and Kerala copper plates.
materials_techniques: stone inscription; wall painting
leaves_out: "Nestorian" is a label by opponents; Syriac Christians of Kerala
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Sunni Islam
making_significance: Sunni practice commissions mosques, minbars, Qur'an manuscripts, calligraphy and endowed (waqf) complexes across the Islamic world.
materials_techniques: calligraphy; manuscript illumination; architecture; tilework
functions: ritual and belief;record and writing;rule and display
leaves_out: non-Muslim makers of mosque fittings; figurative traditions; diverse regional practice
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Walters Art Museum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;Qatar Digital Library

name: Shiʻi Islam
making_significance: Shiʻi practice commissioned shrines such as Mashhad and Karbala, Muharram standards (alams) and ta'ziyeh passion-play material.
materials_techniques: metal standards; tilework; mirror mosaic; textile banners
leaves_out: Ismaili and Zaydi traditions often subsumed; South Asian Muharram arts
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Ibadi Islam
making_significance: Ibadi communities in Oman and the M'zab valley built austere mosques and settlements later admired by modernist architects.
materials_techniques: mudbrick and lime building
leaves_out: M'zab women's weaving; Omani craft
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: Le Corbusier's interest in M'zab is widely reported.

name: Sufi orders
other_names: tariqas (Chishti, Mevlevi, Qadiri, Tijani and others)
making_significance: Sufi orders commissioned shrines, lodges and devotional objects, from Mevlevi dress and instruments to Mouride portraits in Senegal and Chishti shrine textiles.
materials_techniques: shrine building; calligraphy; textiles; music
functions: ritual and belief;play and music;clothing and adornment
leaves_out: women and non-elite devotees; suppression in Turkey (1925) and elsewhere
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Theravada Buddhism
making_significance: Theravada communities in Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia commission stupas, Buddha images, palm-leaf manuscripts and merit-making textiles.
materials_techniques: bronze casting; lacquer and gilding; palm-leaf writing; brick stupas
leaves_out: women's merit-weaving; images removed from temples to collections
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Mahayana Buddhism
making_significance: Mahayana practice drove cave temples, bronze and wood bodhisattvas, sutra copying and woodblock printing, including the earliest dated printed book (868).
materials_techniques: woodblock printing; bronze and wood sculpture; sutra copying; cave carving
leaves_out: lay women patrons; the removal of cave murals and heads to foreign collections
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1);ColBase Japan (Japan Government Standard Terms);Wikimedia Commons

name: Vajrayana Buddhism
making_significance: Vajrayana monasteries commission thangka paintings, gilt-copper images, sand mandalas and ritual implements following precise iconometric rules.
materials_techniques: thangka painting; gilt-copper casting; appliqué; sand mandala
leaves_out: Newar artists who made much of it; objects sold after 1959; initiation-restricted images
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Himalayan Art Resources (link out);Rijksmuseum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Chan and Zen Buddhism
making_significance: Chan and Zen monasteries shaped ink painting, calligraphy, dry gardens and tea practice.
materials_techniques: ink painting; calligraphy; garden making; tea ceramics
defined_by: the monasteries; scholars; D. T. Suzuki's Western framing
leaves_out: the Western "Zen aesthetic" simplification; lay and commercial makers
free_sources: ColBase Japan (Japan Government Standard Terms);Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Shaiva traditions
making_significance: Shaiva devotion commissioned lingas, temples and processional bronzes such as the Chola Nataraja.
materials_techniques: lost-wax bronze; granite carving
leaves_out: temple servants and dancers; stolen temple images in Western museums
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Vaishnava traditions
making_significance: Vaishnava devotion produced Krishna paintings, pichhvai temple hangings and Jagannath imagery.
materials_techniques: opaque watercolour; temple cloth painting
leaves_out: temple painters of Nathdwara; lower-caste devotees
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Shakta traditions
making_significance: Goddess worship shaped Durga festival images of clay made each year and temples to Kali and the Mahavidyas.
materials_techniques: unfired clay modelling; painting
leaves_out: Kumartuli image-makers (Kolkata); tantric practice
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Jainism
making_significance: Jain merchants funded marble temples such as Dilwara and Ranakpur and illustrated Kalpasutra manuscripts.
materials_techniques: marble carving; manuscript painting; cloth paintings
leaves_out: temple carvers; Digambara and Svetambara difference
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Sikhism
making_significance: Sikh practice centres on the Guru Granth Sahib, gurdwaras such as the Harmandir Sahib, and arms and dress of the Khalsa.
materials_techniques: manuscript copying; gilding; weaponry
leaves_out: objects taken 1849; Sikh women's roles
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Daoism
making_significance: Daoist institutions commissioned ritual paintings, robes, talismans and temple images.
materials_techniques: embroidery; painting; woodblock
leaves_out: local cults; women practitioners
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Confucian ritual
making_significance: Confucian ritual fixed ancestor-hall furniture, ritual bronzes and ceramics, and Korea's Jongmyo royal rites.
materials_techniques: ritual vessels; lacquer
leaves_out: women's labour in ancestral rites; non-elite practice
free_sources: National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1);Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Treated as ritual practice, not a church.

name: Shinto
making_significance: Shinto shrines rebuild Ise every 20 years and commission mirrors, swords and festival floats.
materials_techniques: cypress carpentry; metalwork; float making
defined_by: priests; scholars; the Meiji state (State Shinto)
leaves_out: the Meiji separation of Buddhism; local kami; Ainu and Ryukyu
free_sources: ColBase Japan (Japan Government Standard Terms);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Ise rebuilding is a case for repair and renewal.

name: Bon
making_significance: Bon monasteries produce thangkas, images and ritual objects parallel to Buddhist ones.
materials_techniques: painting; casting
leaves_out: pre-Buddhist religion confused with organised Bon
free_sources: Himalayan Art Resources (link out);Wikimedia Commons

name: Korean shamanism
making_significance: Korean mudang (shamans) use painted deity portraits, costumes, fans and paper decorations in gut rituals.
materials_techniques: painting; paper craft; costume
leaves_out: women practitioners as makers; suppression under Joseon, colonial and modern states
free_sources: National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1);Wikimedia Commons

name: Chinese popular religion
making_significance: Popular religion drives paper offerings burned for the dead, temple images, door gods and New Year prints.
materials_techniques: paper craft; woodblock printing; temple carving
leaves_out: diaspora temples; paper-offering makers
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data

name: Shamanic traditions of Siberia and the steppe
date_note: c.; long histories, documented from 17th c.; continue and revive after 1991
making_significance: Siberian and steppe practitioners (Evenki, Sakha, Buryat, Tuvan and others) make frame drums, costumes hung with iron pendants and spirit figures that are also regular targets of collecting.
materials_techniques: frame-drum making; skin sewing; iron pendant forging; carved spirit figures
functions: ritual and belief;play and music;care and access
defined_by: anthropologists; the Evenki word šaman borrowed via Russian into a general term
leaves_out: the term's flattening of distinct peoples' practices; Soviet persecution and confiscations; objects held in St Petersburg and elsewhere
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: Term "shamanism" is an outsiders' generalisation; use each people's own terms where possible.

name: Mesoamerican religion
date_note: c.; Olmec period to conquest; many practices continue in syncretic forms
making_significance: Mesoamerican ritual shaped codices of the 260-day calendar, ball courts, incense burners, offerings of jade and feathers, and bloodletting implements.
materials_techniques: screenfold painting; jade carving; featherwork; ceramic incense burners
functions: ritual and belief;record and writing;play and music
leaves_out: Indigenous present-day practitioners; destruction of codices by missionaries (Maní 1562)
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);LACMA (public-domain images);Wikimedia Commons

name: Andean religion (huacas)
making_significance: Andean ritual made offerings of cloth, spondylus shell, miniature figures and keros to huacas (sacred places and beings) and ancestors.
materials_techniques: tapestry offerings; spondylus working; metal miniatures
leaves_out: the huacas themselves as persons; present Quechua and Aymara practice
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Pueblo religion (katsina)
making_significance: Hopi and Zuni carvers make katsina figures (tihu) and masks, the latter ceremonial and not for sale or display.
materials_techniques: cottonwood root carving; painting
leaves_out: masks sold at auction against tribal objection; carvers as named artists
free_sources: community-published site

name: Ghost Dance
making_significance: Ghost Dance followers painted muslin and hide shirts and dresses, some taken from the dead at Wounded Knee (1890).
materials_techniques: painting on muslin and hide
leaves_out: the Wounded Knee dead; Lakota requests for return
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items)
notes: Glasgow returned a Ghost Dance shirt in 1999.

name: Native American Church
making_significance: Native American Church members make beaded ritual fans, gourd rattles and staffs for peyote meetings.
materials_techniques: beadwork (gourd stitch); featherwork
leaves_out: ritual use protected only from 1994; sacred content
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items)

name: Yorùbá religion
other_names: Òrìṣà worship; Ifá divination; diaspora branches include Lucumí (Santería/Regla de Ocha) in Cuba
date_note: c.; continues in West Africa and the Americas
making_significance: Òrìṣà shrines and Ifá diviners commission carved divination trays and bowls, beaded crowns, twin figures (ère ìbejì) and shrine sculpture.
materials_techniques: wood carving; beadwork; brass
object_types: Ifá trays; ère ìbejì; beaded crowns
leaves_out: named carvers (e.g. Olowe of Ise); diaspora practitioners
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Ifá is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list (2008).

name: Vodun (Fon, Ewe and Gbe-speaking peoples)
date_note: c.; older roots; continues in Benin, Togo and Ghana
making_significance: Vodun practice sustains shrines, bocio empowered figures, appliqué and metal emblems for deities, some of which also served the Dahomey court.
materials_techniques: wood carving; assemblage with cord and cloth; iron and brass forging
functions: ritual and belief;care and access;rule and display
leaves_out: practitioners' own names for objects; objects removed as "fetishes"; Vodun's link to the Atlantic trade framed without people
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Benin's national Vodun day (10 January) since 1996.

name: Akan religion
making_significance: Akan religious practice includes shrines to abosom, akuaba figures carried for fertility, and terracotta memorial heads made by women potters.
materials_techniques: wood carving; terracotta modelling; brass casting
leaves_out: women potters of memorial heads; Christian and Muslim Akan; objects dug from burial sites for the art market
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Memorial heads are often looted from graves.

name: Kongo religion and minkisi
date_note: c.; continues; carried to the Americas
making_significance: Kongo ritual specialists (nganga) assembled minkisi, including nail-driven nkisi nkondi, and Kongo grave decoration travelled to the Americas with enslaved people.
materials_techniques: wood carving; assemblage with medicines; nailing; grave decoration
functions: ritual and belief;care and access;rule and display
leaves_out: nganga as named makers; "fetish" framing; people whose knowledge crossed the Atlantic in slavery
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);AfricaMuseum Tervuren collection search (link out);Wikimedia Commons

name: Candomblé
other_names: Candomblé Ketu, Jeje and Angola nations
date_note: c.; earliest terreiros in Bahia in the 19th c.; continues
making_significance: Candomblé houses make beaded necklaces (fios de conta), ritual dress, metal tools and altars for the orixás, inkices and voduns.
materials_techniques: glass beadwork; embroidery and lace; forged and cut metal
leaves_out: women priestesses (mães-de-santo) as leaders and makers; police seizures (Rio objects transferred to Museu da República in 2020)
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;community-published site

name: Haitian Vodou
making_significance: Haitian Vodou artists sew sequinned drapo (flags) for the lwa, cut oil-drum iron sculpture and draw vèvè ground designs.
materials_techniques: sequin and bead embroidery; cut steel drums; cornmeal drawing
leaves_out: the anti-superstition campaigns (1941–42) that destroyed objects; Hollywood stereotypes
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items)

name: Rastafari
making_significance: Rastafari shaped Jamaican dress (crocheted tams), wood carving and reggae record-sleeve art in red, gold and green.
materials_techniques: crochet; wood carving; graphic design
functions: ritual and belief;clothing and adornment;play and music
leaves_out: women in the movement; persecution such as the Coral Gardens incident (1963); commercial use of its colours
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Malagasy ancestral religion
making_significance: Malagasy ancestor practice wraps the dead in silk lamba mena during famadihana reburials, and in the south carved aloalo posts mark Mahafaly tombs.
materials_techniques: silk weaving; wood carving; tomb building
leaves_out: Christian Malagasy; aloalo removed from tombs for sale
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Aboriginal Dreaming
other_names: the Dreaming; Jukurrpa (Warlpiri); Tjukurpa (Anangu); many other language terms
date_note: deep time, as the communities describe it; continues
making_significance: Aboriginal law and story are expressed through rock art, body and ground designs, bark and acrylic painting and ceremonial objects, with rules about who may make and see them.
materials_techniques: ochre painting; bark painting; acrylic painting; fibre
functions: ritual and belief;record and writing;rule and display
defined_by: Aboriginal communities themselves; "Dreaming/Dreamtime" was coined by outsiders (Spencer and Gillen, Stanner)
leaves_out: restricted and secret-sacred knowledge; distinct language groups flattened into one term; communities' own words
free_sources: Museums Victoria Collections (CC BY or public domain where marked);community-published site
notes: Use each community's own term; restricted objects never displayed.

name: Māori customary and spiritual practice
date_note: c.; since settlement of Aotearoa; continues
making_significance: Tikanga governs how whakairo (carving), raranga (weaving) and tā moko are made and how taonga (treasured objects) are cared for, including their return.
materials_techniques: wood carving; flax weaving; tattooing; greenstone working
functions: ritual and belief;clothing and adornment;rule and display
leaves_out: iwi as peoples not states; distinct iwi practices; toi moko (preserved heads) repatriation
free_sources: Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked);Auckland Museum Collections Online (CC BY where marked);community-published site
notes: Not a "religion" in the church sense: customary law and practice.

name: Hawaiian religion
date_note: c.; kapu system abolished 1819; practices revived since 1970s
making_significance: Hawaiian religion commissioned carved temple images (kiʻi), feathered god images (akua hulu manu) and heiau.
materials_techniques: wood carving; featherwork on basketry; stone platform building
leaves_out: images burned in 1819; present Hawaiian practitioners; objects in Western museums
free_sources: community-published site;Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items)

name: Sámi religion
making_significance: Sámi noaidi used painted frame drums, many confiscated by Lutheran authorities, one of which was returned from Denmark in 2023.
materials_techniques: frame drums with alder-bark paint; carving
leaves_out: Sámi across four states; the drums' owners (e.g. Bendix Ivarsen's drum taken 1691)
free_sources: Finna.fi (CC BY where marked);Wikimedia Commons

name: Baháʼí Faith
making_significance: The Baháʼí Faith commissions terraced gardens and nine-sided temples such as the Lotus Temple in Delhi (1986).
materials_techniques: reinforced concrete; marble cladding; garden design
leaves_out: persecution in Iran; local architects
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Malagan (New Ireland)
date_note: c.; documented from the 19th c., older roots; continues
making_significance: Malagan ceremonies in New Ireland commission carved and painted figures and friezes to honour the dead, made to be displayed once and then left to decay or, from the colonial period, sold, which is why museums hold so many.
materials_techniques: wood carving; painting with ochres and lime; fibre
leaves_out: carvers' rights to specific designs (owned as intellectual property); objects meant to decay; communities' present practice
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Auckland Museum Collections Online (CC BY where marked);Wikimedia Commons
notes: A ceremonial complex rather than a religion; design rights are transmitted and owned.
